newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FOCUS-AT&T partner out of Ivory Coast phone bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-AT&T partner out of Ivory Coast phone bid.

text.p: The battle for the takeover of Ivory Coast's telephone company CI-TELCOM took a dramatic turn on Thursday when local consortium Africa Bell, which chose U.S. telecommunications giant AT&T as its partners, was disqualified from bidding.

"The decision to disqualify Africa Bell was taken by the Privatisation Committee," committee president Jean-Claude Brou told reporters. "Africa Bell had not demonstrated technical or financial capacity."

Africa Bell President Hamed Bassam told a news conference his group protested to the Ivorian president and parliament, claiming unfair treatment. He said his consortium met all the conditions given the limited time it had to do so.

"It is extremely retgrettable and prejudicial for national interest that the decision to disqualify the only Ivorian operator has been taken, apparently outside any economic or technical consideration," Bassam said.

AT&T's Director of Programmes for Sub-Saharan Africa, Karen Freeman, told Reuters at the news conference that AT&T was disappointed by the decision, although its option on 35 percent of Africa Bell's capital was still being studied internally.
"It's Africa Bell's bid. As potential technical contractors to them, that relationship still exists," she said.
Brou said during a round of bidding on December 17, when France Telecom and Telekom Malaysia also made offers, that Africa Bell did not yet have a reputable technical partner.
"Africa Bell also wrote at the time to say its financial plan had not yet been concluded," Brou added.

A partner in Africa Bell, founded by Ivorian entities, announced on Monday that AT&T had since given a firm commitment to take up a 35 percent stake and make its technical expertise available to the consortium.
The elimination of Africa Bell, announced at a final round of bidding, leaves the French and the Malaysians as the only contenders for a 51 percent strategic stake in CI-TELCOM.

France Telecom, bidding through a local consortium led by its subsidiary, France Cable Radio, this time offered 105 billion CFA francs ($198 million) for the 204,000 shares on sale, an improvement of two billion CFA on its previous bid.

It also repeated an offer to pay off 40 billion CFA of CI-TELCOM's debt over 10 years and to finance the network with a 25 billion CFA loan it was arranging through institutional partners in Africa and Europe. Telekom Malaysia made a significant increase in its previous offer of 82.4 billion CFA for the shares, raising it to 104 billion CFA. Like the French, the Malaysians agreed to recapitalise 51 percent of CI-TELCOM.
France Telecom is counting on its long association with Ivory Coast, a former French colony, where the French network is a major supplier, technical partner and creditor.

The local consortium through which it bid includes diversified group SIFCOM, the largest private company in Ivory Coast, with interests ranging from commodities to car dealerships and duty-free shops.
